opus-5.5.text:
I think one of the most interesting potential benefits is diversity. Each model family ends up with its own quirks: different pretraining data mixtures, different tokenizers, different architectural choices, and different post-training recipes. So when you train or distill across several families, rather than within a single lineage, you're exposing the learning process to a broader range of "views" on the same problem.

Concretely, there are a few ways that can pay off. One is robustness. If you generate synthetic data or reasoning traces from just one model, you tend to inherit that model's blind spots and stylistic habits, and in the worst case you get a kind of collapse where everything starts to look the same. Mixing sources from different families tends to smooth out those idiosyncrasies, so the resulting model generalizes better instead of just imitating one teacher.

A second benefit is complementary strengths. One family might be stronger at code, another at multilingual tasks, another at long-form reasoning. If you can combine signals from all of them, you can get a student or a merged model that's better across the board than any single source.

And third, from a research perspective, it helps you separate what's actually a general property of the method from what's an artifact of one particular model. If a training recipe works across, say, Llama-style, Qwen-style, and other open families, you have much more confidence that you've found something real rather than something that only works because of how one base model happened to be pretrained.

The caveat is that it's not free. Different tokenizers and output formats can make things messier, and naive mixing can sometimes hurt if the sources disagree in inconsistent ways. So you need to be thoughtful about filtering and curation. But overall, I think the diversity you gain is often worth that extra effort.

r001.rationale: The response says model families can have complementary strengths, such as code, multilingual tasks, and reasoning, and that combining their signals can produce a stronger model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so one thing I find really exciting about training across multiple model families is that it lets you separate what's actually a general insight from what's just an artifact of one particular model. A lot of the research in this space ends up being done on a single family, say one base model at a couple of sizes, and then people draw conclusions about scaling or about data mixtures or about test-time compute, and it's really hard to know whether those conclusions transfer. If you run the same recipe on, say, a Qwen model, a Llama model, and a Gemma model, and you see the same trend, you have much more confidence that you're learning something about the method rather than about some quirk of that pretraining data or that tokenizer or that architecture.

The second benefit is more practical. Different model families have different strengths coming out of pretraining. Some are much stronger at math or code, some have better multilingual coverage, some are more amenable to being fine-tuned with very little data. When we did the s1 work on simple test-time scaling, for example, we saw that the base model mattered a lot for how far you could get with a tiny amount of supervised fine-tuning data. Training across families gives you a sense of where the ceiling is coming from, the data or the recipe, versus the starting point.

And then there's a community benefit. If you only show results on one family, people who are building on a different one don't know if they should trust your findings. Showing that something holds across families makes the work far more useful and much more likely to actually get adopted. It's more compute, obviously, so you have to be deliberate about where you spend it, but I think for anything that's claiming to be a general method, having at least a couple of families in the mix is really worth it.

r001.rationale: The response notes that model families have different strengths, but describes comparing them to understand results and starting points. It does not say that combining those strengths provides an ensemble-like benefit.

astra-6.text: I think one potential benefit is that insights can transfer across model families. If you work on an encoder, a decoder, and an encoder-decoder model, you can get a better sense of which training choices are broadly useful and which are specific to an architecture. That can help you bring improvements from one family into another, and also choose the right architecture for the task rather than assuming one approach is always best.

r001.rationale: The response describes transferring training insights across architectures and choosing an architecture for a task. It does not suggest an ensemble-like benefit from combining the model families’ different strengths.

sol-6.1.text: I think one potential benefit is that different model families may learn different things, even when they’re trained on similar data. They have different architectures and training recipes, so their strengths and weaknesses can be complementary. If you can transfer knowledge across those families, you might get a model that generalizes better than one that only learns from models very similar to itself. The interesting question is how much of that diversity actually translates into better performance.

r001.rationale: The response says different families have complementary strengths and that transferring knowledge across them could produce a better-generalizing model, conveying ensemble-like benefits from combining their strengths.
